own_scenes.desc: Greg Mack llegó de Houston en 1983 para salvar KDAY 1580-AM, la última de las cinco emisoras negras de la ciudad; abrió la ventana de su casa en South Central, oyó Run-DMC y Kurtis Blow en todos los coches y puso rap: en el primer sondeo pasaron a segundos. Rodger Clayton le despreció («¿parece que necesito la radio?») y se alió con Alonzo Williams: sus «Mack Attack Mixmasters» y el «Traffic Jam» pusieron en antena las mezclas de cuatro pistas de Dr. Dre y Yella, que se vendían en el Roadium Swap Meet. Sin payola y con las puertas abiertas, rompió casi todos los grupos de la Costa Oeste (Yo-Yo, Sir Jinx, N.W.A) y también el freestyle; organizaba bailes en las pistas de patinaje, baratas y con buen sonido, rotando territorios: Skateland (Bloods, en Compton), World on Wheels (Crips), Sherman Square (bandas latinas), la Casa Camino Real como terreno neutral y el 321 Club para los chicos blancos. Las bandas lo respetaban y hasta le llamaban para explicar sus tiroteos. «Sin KDAY no sería quien soy» (Murs).

influences.name: Electro de Los Ángeles: Wreckin’ Cru y Uncle Jamm’s Army

refs.q: It didn’t take long to figure out just by opening your window what everybody was listening to, which was rap music.
refs.para: I said, “Let me listen to what’s going on in the city,” because I didn’t really know the city that well yet. I was living with my mom. She had a rental house behind her house in South Central L.A. It didn’t take long to figure out just by opening your window what everybody was listening to, which was rap music. Everywhere. You’d hear cars bumping through the neighborhood playing Run-DMC or Kurtis Blow.

refs.q: Because it wasn’t just two turntables. Dre actually made it a production.
refs.para: I listened to their mix. I was blown away. I was like, “Oh my God.” Because it wasn’t just two turntables. Dre actually made it a production. It was like an eight-track, a mix. Dre would actually lay a beat down for thirty minutes, then he’d come back and layer some other music over that, layer some other music over that. I’d never heard nothing like it.

refs.q: It was what everybody Black listened to. It was everything for us.
refs.para: Ice Cube (artist, N.W.A): [KDAY] was so big that all we dreamed of was to have a song playing on KDAY. It was what everybody Black listened to. It was everything for us.

refs.q: I wouldn’t be who I am without KDAY.
refs.para: Murs (artist, Los Angeles): It was a godsend. They’d broadcast the Ten Commandments every day. Religiously listening, taping, especially for someone like me—there was no other way that I was getting rap music into my house. My mom would throw away my tapes. And as a child from a low-income family with no income, it was almost impossible for me to get rap music. I wouldn’t be who I am without KDAY.
